nameStory: Actidesmium hookeri is named after the renowned 19th-century botanist William Jackson Hooker, who made significant contributions to botanical science. The genus name 'Actidesmium' comes from Greek words meaning 'ray bundle,' referring to how these microscopic algae cells arrange themselves in radiating clusters.
description: **UNCERTAIN IDENTIFICATION** Actidesmium hookeri is a microscopic freshwater green alga that forms tiny colonies in New England waters. These single-celled organisms group together in small, spherical clusters that are barely visible to the naked eye. Each colony might be smaller than a pinhead, containing dozens of individual cells arranged in a geometric pattern. You'll need a hand lens or microscope to truly appreciate their intricate structure.

idTips.label: Colony structure
idTips.description: Forms small, round clusters of cells that look like tiny green specks floating in water - use a 10x hand lens to see the radiating pattern of individual cells

idTips.label: Cell arrangement
idTips.description: Individual cells within colonies are arranged in a spoke-like pattern, radiating outward from the center like bicycle wheel spokes

idTips.label: Size scale
idTips.description: Colonies are extremely small - about the size of a grain of fine sand or smaller, requiring magnification to observe details

idTips.label: Color appearance
idTips.description: Bright green color that may appear as a faint greenish tint in the water when colonies are present in large numbers

habitat: **UNCERTAIN** Found in clean, cool freshwater environments like pristine ponds, slow-moving streams, and the shallow edges of clear lakes throughout New England. Prefers areas with good water quality and may be more common in higher elevation or less disturbed aquatic habitats.

funFact: Despite being incredibly tiny, Actidesmium hookeri has only been documented twice in all of New England, making it rarer to spot than a snowy owl or a wild orchid - yet it might be living in your local pond right now, invisible to the naked eye!
confusionNotes: **UNCERTAIN** Could be confused with other microscopic green algae colonies, but the distinctive radiating cell pattern within spherical colonies helps distinguish it from randomly arranged colonial algae.
contextualKnowledge: This species represents the incredible hidden diversity of microscopic life in New England waters - there are likely thousands of algae species living in our region that most people never notice or consider part of our local flora.
